questions.title: Shopper contact list
questions.difficultyWhy: One table, two named columns, no filtering.
questions.prompt: Return the name and email of every shopper.
questions.rationale: Choose specific columns with SELECT. One table, two named columns, no filtering.
edgeCases: Include shoppers whose email is missing (it shows as NULL).
hints: List the two columns after SELECT, separated by a comma.
The table is shoppers.
questions.solution: SELECT name, email FROM shoppers

questions.title: Shoppers in the West region
questions.difficultyWhy: A single equality filter on one table.
questions.prompt: Return the id and name of shoppers whose region is West.
questions.rationale: Filter rows with WHERE and a text value. A single equality filter on one table.
edgeCases: Region values are capitalised exactly as 'West'.
hints: Text values go in single quotes.
WHERE region = 'West'
questions.solution: SELECT id, name FROM shoppers WHERE region = 'West'

questions.title: Catalog from most to least expensive
questions.difficultyWhy: One table and one sort, plus a stated tie-breaker.
questions.prompt: Return the name and price of every catalog item, most expensive first.
questions.rationale: Sort descending and break ties with a second key. One table and one sort, plus a stated tie-breaker.
edgeCases: When two items have the same price, list them by name A→Z.
hints: ORDER BY price DESC puts the highest price first.
Add a second sort key after a comma: , name
questions.solution: SELECT name, price FROM catalog_items ORDER BY price DESC, name

questions.title: Orders with no delivery date
questions.difficultyWhy: One IS NULL test on one table.
questions.prompt: Return the id and status of every order whose delivered_date is missing.
questions.rationale: Find missing values with IS NULL. One IS NULL test on one table.
edgeCases: Look at delivered_date itself — one delivered order is missing its date, and it should be included.
rejectedApproaches: uses status instead of the date
hints: NULL never equals anything, so = NULL doesn't work.
Use delivered_date IS NULL.
questions.solution: SELECT id, status FROM sales_orders WHERE delivered_date IS NULL

questions.title: The three cheapest items
questions.difficultyWhy: One sort plus LIMIT on one table.
questions.prompt: Return the name and price of the 3 cheapest catalog items, cheapest first.
questions.rationale: Combine ORDER BY with LIMIT. One sort plus LIMIT on one table.
edgeCases: Break price ties by name A→Z.
hints: Sort ascending by price.
LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows.
questions.solution: SELECT name, price FROM catalog_items ORDER BY price, name LIMIT 3

questions.title: Rename a column
questions.prompt: Return each employee's name and salary, naming the salary column annual_salary.
questions.rationale: Name an output column with AS. One table, one alias.
hints: Write the column, then AS and the new name.
questions.solution: SELECT name, salary AS annual_salary FROM employees

questions.title: Office locations
questions.prompt: Return each department location once (column location).
questions.rationale: Remove duplicate values with DISTINCT. DISTINCT on a single column.
hints: SELECT DISTINCT returns each value once.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT location FROM departments

questions.title: Hired during 2023
questions.difficultyWhy: One inclusive date range on one table.
questions.prompt: Return the name and hired_at of employees hired during 2023.
questions.rationale: Filter an inclusive date range. One inclusive date range on one table.
edgeCases: Include 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2023. Dates are stored as YYYY-MM-DD text.
hints: BETWEEN includes both ends.
questions.solution: SELECT name, hired_at FROM employees WHERE hired_at BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31'

questions.title: Orders by status
questions.difficultyWhy: One GROUP BY with COUNT on one table.
questions.prompt: Return each order status and how many orders have it (order_count).
questions.rationale: Count rows per group. One GROUP BY with COUNT on one table.
hints: GROUP BY status makes one row per status.
COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group.
questions.solution: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM sales_orders GROUP BY status

questions.title: Items nobody has ordered
questions.difficultyWhy: A LEFT JOIN anti-join between two tables.
questions.prompt: Return the id and name of catalog items that appear on no order line.
questions.rationale: Find rows with no match in another table. A LEFT JOIN anti-join between two tables.
edgeCases: Any order line counts, whatever the order's status.
hints: LEFT JOIN keeps every catalog item, even without matching lines.
Items with no match have NULL in the joined columns.
questions.solution: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM catalog_items c LEFT JOIN order_lines l ON l.item_id = c.id WHERE l.item_id IS NULL

questions.title: Repeat shoppers
questions.difficultyWhy: GROUP BY with a HAVING condition on one table.
questions.prompt: Return shopper_id and order_count for shoppers who placed at least 2 orders.
questions.rationale: Filter groups with HAVING. GROUP BY with a HAVING condition on one table.
edgeCases: Count orders of every status, including cancelled ones.
hints: Group by shopper_id.
HAVING filters after counting: HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2.
questions.solution: SELECT shopper_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM sales_orders GROUP BY shopper_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2

questions.title: Delivered revenue by category
questions.difficultyWhy: Two joins and one SUM per group; no nesting.
questions.prompt: For delivered orders only, return category and revenue: the sum of quantity × unit_price from order_lines.
questions.rationale: Aggregate a calculated value across joined tables. Two joins and one SUM per group; no nesting.
edgeCases: Use order_lines.unit_price (what was charged), not the catalog's current price.
Round revenue to 2 decimals.
hints: Join order_lines to sales_orders for the status and to catalog_items for the category.
ROUND(SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price), 2)
questions.solution: SELECT c.category, ROUND(SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price), 2) AS revenue FROM order_lines l JOIN sales_orders o ON o.id = l.order_id JOIN catalog_items c ON c.id = l.item_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.category

questions.title: Signups in the last 30 days
questions.difficultyWhy: One table, but the inclusive 30-day window must be worked out.
questions.prompt: Return the name and signup_date of shoppers who signed up in the 30 days ending on 2025-03-31.
questions.rationale: Turn a rolling period into exact date boundaries. One table, but the inclusive 30-day window must be worked out.
edgeCases: The 30 days are 2025-03-02 through 2025-03-31, both included.
hints: Both ends are included.
date('2025-03-31', '-29 days') gives the first day.
questions.solution: SELECT name, signup_date FROM shoppers WHERE signup_date BETWEEN '2025-03-02' AND '2025-03-31'

questions.title: Emails used more than once
questions.difficultyWhy: String normalisation plus GROUP BY/HAVING on one table.
questions.prompt: Some shoppers share an email once you ignore letter case and surrounding spaces. Return clean_email and shopper_count for every such email used by more than one shopper.
questions.rationale: Normalise text before comparing it. String normalisation plus GROUP BY/HAVING on one table.
edgeCases: clean_email = the email trimmed and lowercased.
Ignore shoppers with no email.
hints: LOWER(TRIM(email)) normalises an email.
Group by the cleaned value and keep groups with COUNT(*) > 1.
questions.solution: SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email, COUNT(*) AS shopper_count FROM shoppers WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

questions.title: Employees and their departments
questions.difficultyWhy: One INNER JOIN on a foreign key.
questions.prompt: Return employee (the employee's name) and department (the department's name) for employees who belong to a department.
questions.rationale: Join two tables on a key. One INNER JOIN on a foreign key.
edgeCases: Employees without a department are not listed.
hints: Match employees.department_id to departments.id.
Both tables have a name column — alias them.
questions.solution: SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id

questions.title: Every employee, with a department label
questions.difficultyWhy: LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE for the missing side.
questions.prompt: Return employee and department for every employee. Use 'Unassigned' as the department when an employee has none.
questions.rationale: Keep unmatched rows and label them. LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE for the missing side.
hints: LEFT JOIN keeps employees with no matching department.
COALESCE(d.name, 'Unassigned')
questions.solution: SELECT e.name AS employee, COALESCE(d.name, 'Unassigned') AS department FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id

questions.title: Find the lamps
questions.difficultyWhy: One LIKE pattern, but case behaviour matters.
questions.prompt: Return the id and name of catalog items whose name contains “lamp” anywhere, in any letter case.
questions.rationale: Search text with LIKE and wildcards. One LIKE pattern, but case behaviour matters.
edgeCases: “Desk Lamp” and “Floor lamp” both count.
hints: % matches any run of characters.
SQLite's LIKE ignores case for English letters.
questions.solution: SELECT id, name FROM catalog_items WHERE name LIKE '%lamp%'

questions.title: Open orders in February and March
questions.difficultyWhy: IN plus BETWEEN combined correctly; operator precedence is the trap.
questions.prompt: Return id, status and order_date for orders that are shipped or processing and were placed from 2025-02-01 through 2025-03-31.
questions.rationale: Combine conditions without precedence mistakes. IN plus BETWEEN combined correctly; operator precedence is the trap.
edgeCases: Both boundary dates are included.
hints: status IN ('shipped', 'processing') avoids an OR.
If you use OR, wrap it in parentheses.
questions.solution: SELECT id, status, order_date FROM sales_orders WHERE status IN ('shipped', 'processing') AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-02-01' AND '2025-03-31'

questions.title: Average salary by department
questions.difficultyWhy: One join, one AVG per group, rounding.
questions.prompt: Return department (name) and avg_salary for every department that has at least one employee.
questions.rationale: Average per group across a join. One join, one AVG per group, rounding.
edgeCases: Round avg_salary to 2 decimals.
hints: Join, then GROUP BY the department.
ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2)
questions.solution: SELECT d.name AS department, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id GROUP BY d.id

questions.title: Price bands
questions.difficultyWhy: A three-way CASE with exact boundaries.
questions.prompt: Return name and price_band for every catalog item: 'budget' when price is under 25, 'standard' from 25 up to (not including) 100, 'premium' at 100 or more.
questions.rationale: Bucket values with CASE. A three-way CASE with exact boundaries.
edgeCases: An item priced exactly 25 is standard.
hints: CASE checks its WHEN branches top to bottom.
WHEN price < 25 THEN 'budget' WHEN price < 100 THEN 'standard' ELSE 'premium'
questions.solution: SELECT name, CASE WHEN price < 25 THEN 'budget' WHEN price < 100 THEN 'standard' ELSE 'premium' END AS price_band FROM catalog_items

questions.title: Active buyers per month
questions.difficultyWhy: Month bucketing plus a distinct count, one table.
questions.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and active_shoppers: how many different shoppers placed at least one non-cancelled order that month.
questions.rationale: Count distinct people per calendar month. Month bucketing plus a distinct count, one table.
edgeCases: Cancelled orders don't count.
A shopper with several orders in a month counts once.
hints: strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) gives the month.
COUNT(DISTINCT shopper_id)
questions.solution: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, COUNT(DISTINCT shopper_id) AS active_shoppers FROM sales_orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY month

questions.title: How long did delivery take?
questions.difficultyWhy: One date difference with a NULL guard.
questions.prompt: For delivered orders that have a delivered_date, return id and days_to_deliver: the number of whole days from order_date to delivered_date.
questions.rationale: Subtract dates correctly in SQLite. One date difference with a NULL guard.
edgeCases: Skip orders without a delivered_date.
Return a whole number (integer).
rejectedApproaches: keeps the order with no date
hints: Dates are text: subtracting them directly doesn't work.
CAST(julianday(delivered_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER)
questions.solution: SELECT id, CAST(julianday(delivered_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_to_deliver FROM sales_orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND delivered_date IS NOT NULL

questions.title: Create a wishlist table
questions.difficultyWhy: One CREATE TABLE with a composite key and two inserts.
questions.prompt: Create a table wishlist with shopper_id INTEGER NOT NULL, item_id INTEGER NOT NULL and added_on TEXT, where (shopper_id, item_id) is the primary key. Insert (1, 12, '2025-03-01') and (2, 4, '2025-03-02'), then return all wishlist rows ordered by shopper_id.
questions.rationale: Define a table with a composite primary key and NOT NULL columns. One CREATE TABLE with a composite key and two inserts.
edgeCases: The same shopper can't list the same item twice.
Neither id may be NULL.
hints: PRIMARY KEY(shopper_id, item_id) goes after the column list.
End the script with SELECT * FROM wishlist ORDER BY shopper_id;
questions.solution: CREATE TABLE wishlist(shopper_id INTEGER NOT NULL, item_id INTEGER NOT NULL, added_on TEXT, PRIMARY KEY(shopper_id, item_id)); INSERT INTO wishlist VALUES (1, 12, '2025-03-01'), (2, 4, '2025-03-02'); SELECT shopper_id, item_id, added_on FROM wishlist ORDER BY shopper_id;

questions.title: Reprice the garden range
questions.difficultyWhy: One UPDATE and one DELETE with WHERE, then a SELECT.
questions.prompt: Raise the price of every Garden item by 10%, and delete the item named 'Wall Clock' (it was never sold). Then return id, name and price of all catalog items.
questions.rationale: Change and remove rows safely with WHERE. One UPDATE and one DELETE with WHERE, then a SELECT.
edgeCases: Round price to 2 decimals in the output.
Other categories keep their prices.
hints: UPDATE catalog_items SET price = price * 1.1 WHERE category = 'Garden';
DELETE FROM … WHERE name = 'Wall Clock';
questions.solution: UPDATE catalog_items SET price = price * 1.1 WHERE category = 'Garden'; DELETE FROM catalog_items WHERE name = 'Wall Clock'; SELECT id, name, ROUND(price, 2) AS price FROM catalog_items;

questions.title: Big spenders for their region
questions.difficultyWhy: Aggregate per shopper, then compare with a per-region average (correlated subquery or CTE); NULL regions excluded.
questions.prompt: A shopper's spend is the sum of quantity × unit_price over their delivered orders. Return name, region and spend for shoppers whose spend is greater than the average spend of shoppers in the same region.
questions.rationale: Compare each row with an aggregate of its own group. Aggregate per shopper, then compare with a per-region average (correlated subquery or CTE); NULL regions excluded.
edgeCases: Only shoppers with at least one delivered order are part of a region's average.
Shoppers with no region are excluded.
Round spend to 2 decimals (compare unrounded values).
hints: First compute spend per shopper in a CTE.
Then compare each shopper with AVG(spend) of the same region — a correlated subquery or a second CTE grouped by region.
questions.solution: WITH spend AS (SELECT s.id, s.name, s.region, SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS spend FROM shoppers s JOIN sales_orders o ON o.shopper_id = s.id AND o.status = 'delivered' JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id WHERE s.region IS NOT NULL GROUP BY s.id) SELECT name, region, ROUND(spend, 2) AS spend FROM spend x WHERE spend > (SELECT AVG(spend) FROM spend y WHERE y.region = x.region)

questions.title: Monthly revenue after refunds
questions.difficultyWhy: Two child tables at order grain must be aggregated separately to avoid fan-out; NULL refunds must become 0.
questions.prompt: For delivered orders, return month (YYYY-MM of order_date) and net_revenue: line revenue (quantity × unit_price) minus refunds for those orders.
questions.rationale: Combine line totals and refunds without double counting. Two child tables at order grain must be aggregated separately to avoid fan-out; NULL refunds must become 0.
edgeCases: Orders without refunds subtract 0.
Round net_revenue to 2 decimals.
Months with no delivered orders aren't listed.
hints: Joining lines and refunds directly repeats each refund once per line.
Total lines per order and refunds per order in separate CTEs, then join them to orders.
COALESCE(refund_total, 0)
questions.solution: WITH line AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id), ref AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS refunded FROM order_refunds GROUP BY order_id) SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, ROUND(SUM(l.revenue - COALESCE(r.refunded, 0)), 2) AS net_revenue FROM sales_orders o JOIN line l ON l.order_id = o.id LEFT JOIN ref r ON r.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY month

questions.title: Bestsellers within each category
questions.difficultyWhy: Aggregate after a join, then rank within groups with a stated tie rule.
questions.prompt: For non-cancelled orders, total the units (quantity) sold per catalog item. Return category, name, units and category_rank, where rank 1 is the item with the most units in its category.
questions.rationale: Rank aggregated values per group with DENSE_RANK. Aggregate after a join, then rank within groups with a stated tie rule.
edgeCases: Tied items share a rank and the next rank is not skipped (1, 1, 2).
Items with no units sold are not listed.
hints: First SUM(quantity) per item.
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC)
questions.solution: WITH units AS (SELECT c.category, c.name, SUM(l.quantity) AS units FROM order_lines l JOIN sales_orders o ON o.id = l.order_id JOIN catalog_items c ON c.id = l.item_id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY c.id) SELECT category, name, units, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC) AS category_rank FROM units

questions.title: Seven-day rolling active shoppers
questions.difficultyWhy: Deduplicate to daily counts, then a calendar-based (not row-based) window frame over gaps.
questions.prompt: For each date in app_logins, return login_date, active_shoppers (different shoppers who logged in that day) and rolling_7d: the sum of active_shoppers over that date and the 6 calendar days before it.
questions.rationale: Use a RANGE frame so missing days count as zero. Deduplicate to daily counts, then a calendar-based (not row-based) window frame over gaps.
edgeCases: A shopper logging in twice in a day counts once.
Days with no logins contribute 0 — the window is 7 calendar days, not 7 rows.
hints: COUNT(DISTINCT shopper_id) per login_date first.
ROWS BETWEEN counts rows; with gaps you need a calendar window.
SUM(active) OVER (ORDER BY julianday(login_date) RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
questions.solution: WITH daily AS (SELECT login_date, COUNT(DISTINCT shopper_id) AS active_shoppers FROM app_logins GROUP BY login_date) SELECT login_date, active_shoppers, SUM(active_shoppers) OVER (ORDER BY julianday(login_date) RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_7d FROM daily

questions.title: Above the manager and department benchmark
questions.difficultyWhy: Two role aliases plus an own-group average require two separate comparisons; unknown relationships are excluded.
questions.prompt: Return employee, employee_salary, manager and manager_salary for employees who earn strictly more than both their direct manager and the average salary in their own department. Exclude employees without a department or manager.
questions.rationale: Combine a self join with a correlated department benchmark. Two role aliases plus an own-group average require two separate comparisons; unknown relationships are excluded.
edgeCases: Equal salaries don't count.
Employees without a manager can't qualify.
The department average includes all employees assigned to that department, including the employee being tested.
Both comparisons are strict; equality does not qualify.
rejectedApproaches: Checks only the manager and ignores the department benchmark.
hints: First join each employee to the direct manager.
Compute the department average with a subquery correlated to the employee department. Both comparisons must be true.
questions.solution: SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary AS employee_salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary AND e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.department_id=e.department_id)

questions.title: Days with no orders
questions.difficultyWhy: Requires generating a date series (recursive CTE) and an anti-join against it.
questions.prompt: From 2025-03-01 through 2025-03-14, return each day (column day, YYYY-MM-DD) on which no order was placed, earliest first.
questions.rationale: Find missing dates by building a calendar. Requires generating a date series (recursive CTE) and an anti-join against it.
edgeCases: Both boundary days are included.
Any order status counts as an order.
hints: A table can't show dates it doesn't contain — generate them.
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (SELECT '2025-03-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2025-03-14')
Keep days where NOT EXISTS an order on that date.
questions.solution: WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (SELECT '2025-03-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2025-03-14') SELECT day FROM days WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales_orders o WHERE o.order_date = days.day) ORDER BY day

questions.title: First order versus latest order
questions.difficultyWhy: Order totals, then picking first and last rows per shopper with explicit tie rules.
questions.prompt: For shoppers with at least two non-cancelled orders, return shopper_id, first_order_value and latest_order_value. An order's value is the sum of its lines' quantity × unit_price.
questions.rationale: Pick first and last rows per group, not minimum and maximum values. Order totals, then picking first and last rows per shopper with explicit tie rules.
edgeCases: “First” and “latest” go by order_date; on the same date, the higher order id is later.
Round values to 2 decimals.
hints: Compute each order's value in a CTE.
ROW_NUMBER() per shopper, once ascending and once descending by (order_date, id).
MIN/MAX of the value is not the same as the first/last order.
questions.solution: WITH v AS (SELECT o.id, o.shopper_id, o.order_date, SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS value FROM sales_orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.id), r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY order_date, id) AS first_rn, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, id DESC) AS last_rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id) AS n FROM v) SELECT shopper_id, ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN first_rn = 1 THEN value END), 2) AS first_order_value, ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN last_rn = 1 THEN value END), 2) AS latest_order_value FROM r WHERE n >= 2 GROUP BY shopper_id

questions.title: Orders whose payments don't match
questions.difficultyWhy: Two child tables at different grains (lines, split payments) plus missing payments.
questions.prompt: For delivered or shipped orders, return id, order_total (sum of quantity × unit_price), paid_total (sum of payments) and balance (order_total − paid_total) where paid_total differs from order_total.
questions.rationale: Compare totals from two child tables without fan-out. Two child tables at different grains (lines, split payments) plus missing payments.
edgeCases: Orders with no payment have paid_total 0.
Round all three amounts to 2 decimals and compare the rounded totals.
hints: Some orders have two payments and several lines — join them directly and both repeat.
Sum lines per order and payments per order separately, then LEFT JOIN payments.
questions.solution: WITH t AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS order_total FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id), p AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS paid_total FROM order_payments GROUP BY order_id) SELECT o.id, t.order_total, COALESCE(p.paid_total, 0) AS paid_total, ROUND(t.order_total - COALESCE(p.paid_total, 0), 2) AS balance FROM sales_orders o JOIN t ON t.order_id = o.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status IN ('delivered', 'shipped') AND t.order_total <> COALESCE(p.paid_total, 0)

questions.title: Order status mix by region
questions.difficultyWhy: Pivot with conditional aggregation across a join, plus a NULL group label.
questions.prompt: Return region and four columns — delivered, shipped, processing, cancelled — counting the orders of shoppers in that region with each status.
questions.rationale: Turn rows into columns with SUM(CASE …). Pivot with conditional aggregation across a join, plus a NULL group label.
edgeCases: Shoppers with no region are grouped under 'Unknown'.
A region with no orders of a status shows 0.
hints: SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered
COALESCE(s.region, 'Unknown')
questions.solution: SELECT COALESCE(s.region, 'Unknown') AS region, SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered, SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped, SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'processing' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS processing, SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled FROM sales_orders o JOIN shoppers s ON s.id = o.shopper_id GROUP BY COALESCE(s.region, 'Unknown')

questions.title: Loyal shoppers who never needed a refund
questions.difficultyWhy: Combines a counted EXISTS-style condition with a NOT EXISTS across two hops.
questions.prompt: Return the id and name of shoppers who have at least two delivered orders and have never received a refund on any of their orders.
questions.rationale: Combine “at least N” with “never” conditions. Combines a counted EXISTS-style condition with a NOT EXISTS across two hops.
edgeCases: A refund on any order — delivered or not — disqualifies the shopper.
hints: Count delivered orders with a correlated subquery (or GROUP BY/HAVING).
NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_refunds r JOIN sales_orders o ON o.id = r.order_id WHERE o.shopper_id = s.id)
questions.solution: SELECT s.id, s.name FROM shoppers s WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_orders o WHERE o.shopper_id = s.id AND o.status = 'delivered') >= 2 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_refunds r JOIN sales_orders o ON o.id = r.order_id WHERE o.shopper_id = s.id)

questions.title: Average order value by month
questions.difficultyWhy: The average must be over orders, not lines — a two-step aggregation.
questions.prompt: For delivered orders, return month (YYYY-MM of order_date) and avg_order_value: the average of each order's total (sum of quantity × unit_price).
questions.rationale: Aggregate to the right grain before averaging. The average must be over orders, not lines — a two-step aggregation.
edgeCases: Round to 2 decimals.
hints: AVG over lines averages line values, not orders.
Compute order totals in a CTE first, then AVG them per month.
questions.solution: WITH totals AS (SELECT o.id, strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS total FROM sales_orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.id) SELECT month, ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM totals GROUP BY month

questions.title: Payroll versus budget
questions.difficultyWhy: LEFT JOIN aggregation with zero-filled groups and a strict comparison.
questions.prompt: For every department, return department, headcount, payroll (sum of salaries) and status: 'over' when payroll exceeds the budget, otherwise 'within'.
questions.rationale: Report every group, including empty ones, and classify it. LEFT JOIN aggregation with zero-filled groups and a strict comparison.
edgeCases: Departments with no employees show headcount 0 and payroll 0.
Payroll equal to the budget is 'within'.
hints: Start FROM departments and LEFT JOIN employees.
COUNT(e.id) counts 0 for no matches; COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0).
questions.solution: SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS payroll, CASE WHEN COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) > d.budget THEN 'over' ELSE 'within' END AS status FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id

questions.title: Keep one account per email
questions.difficultyWhy: Normalisation plus a ranked pick per group with a tie-breaker.
questions.prompt: Treat emails as equal after trimming spaces and lowercasing. For each email, keep the shopper who signed up first. Return id, name and clean_email for the kept shoppers.
questions.rationale: Deduplicate by a cleaned key, keeping a defined survivor. Normalisation plus a ranked pick per group with a tie-breaker.
edgeCases: Ties on signup_date go to the lower id.
Shoppers with no email are excluded.
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) ORDER BY signup_date, id)
Keep row number 1.
questions.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT id, name, LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) ORDER BY signup_date, id) AS rn FROM shoppers WHERE email IS NOT NULL) SELECT id, name, clean_email FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1

questions.title: A covering index for unit totals
questions.difficultyWhy: Requires understanding composite index column order, verified on the built index.
questions.prompt: The report “units sold per item” reads order_lines.item_id and quantity. Create an index named idx_lines_item_qty on order_lines that starts with item_id and also contains quantity, so SQLite can answer from the index alone. Then return item_id and units (sum of quantity) per item.
questions.rationale: Design a composite index that covers a query. Requires understanding composite index column order, verified on the built index.
edgeCases: Column order in the index matters: item_id first, then quantity.
hints: CREATE INDEX name ON table(col1, col2);
Use Query Performance to see “USING COVERING INDEX”.
questions.solution: CREATE INDEX idx_lines_item_qty ON order_lines(item_id, quantity); SELECT item_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY item_id;

questions.title: A reusable shopper totals view
questions.difficultyWhy: A view over a join that must count orders, not lines; checked on the view's definition.
questions.prompt: Create a view shopper_order_totals with columns shopper_id, orders (number of non-cancelled orders) and total_spend (sum of quantity × unit_price over those orders, 2 decimals). Then return the view's rows where total_spend is above 150.
questions.rationale: Encapsulate a correct aggregate in a view. A view over a join that must count orders, not lines; checked on the view's definition.
edgeCases: orders counts orders, not order lines.
Only shoppers with at least one non-cancelled order appear in the view.
hints: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT …;
COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) counts orders after joining lines.
questions.solution: CREATE VIEW shopper_order_totals AS SELECT o.shopper_id, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price), 2) AS total_spend FROM sales_orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.shopper_id; SELECT shopper_id, orders, total_spend FROM shopper_order_totals WHERE total_spend > 150;

questions.title: Second-highest salary per department
questions.difficultyWhy: Distinct values, ranking per group, and a NULL result when there is no second value.
questions.prompt: For each department that has employees, return department and second_highest_salary: the second-highest distinct salary in that department.
questions.rationale: Find the Nth distinct value per group, returning NULL when it doesn't exist. Distinct values, ranking per group, and a NULL result when there is no second value.
edgeCases: Equal salaries count once (distinct values).
If a department has only one distinct salary, second_highest_salary is NULL.
rejectedApproaches: ties not treated as one value
drops departments without a second salary
hints: Rank distinct salaries per department with DENSE_RANK … ORDER BY salary DESC.
MAX(CASE WHEN rk = 2 THEN salary END) returns NULL when no rank 2 exists.
questions.solution: WITH r AS (SELECT department_id, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT d.name AS department, MAX(CASE WHEN r.rk = 2 THEN r.salary END) AS second_highest_salary FROM r JOIN departments d ON d.id = r.department_id GROUP BY d.id

questions.title: Next-month retention by signup cohort
questions.difficultyWhy: Cohort assignment, a relative calendar month, an observation cutoff and decimal ratios.
questions.prompt: Group shoppers into cohorts by signup month. A shopper is retained if they placed a non-cancelled order in the calendar month after their signup month. Return cohort_month, cohort_size, retained and retention_pct.
questions.rationale: Build a cohort retention table with a maturity rule. Cohort assignment, a relative calendar month, an observation cutoff and decimal ratios.
edgeCases: cohort_month is YYYY-MM; cohort_size counts every shopper who signed up that month, even those who never ordered.
Only include cohorts whose following month ends on or before 2025-03-31 (later months aren't fully observed).
retention_pct is 0–100 with 2 decimals.
hints: date(signup_month || '-01', '+1 month') gives the first day of the next month.
Flag each shopper 1/0 with EXISTS, then SUM the flags per cohort.
Multiply by 100.0 before dividing to avoid integer division.
questions.solution: WITH c AS (SELECT id, strftime('%Y-%m', signup_date) AS cohort_month FROM shoppers), flagged AS (SELECT c.cohort_month, CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales_orders o WHERE o.shopper_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled' AND strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) = strftime('%Y-%m', c.cohort_month || '-01', '+1 month')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS kept FROM c WHERE date(c.cohort_month || '-01', '+2 months', '-1 day') <= '2025-03-31') SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size, SUM(kept) AS retained, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(kept) / COUNT(*), 2) AS retention_pct FROM flagged GROUP BY cohort_month

questions.title: Longest login streak
questions.difficultyWhy: Gaps-and-islands: deduplicate, derive a group key from dates minus row numbers, then aggregate twice.
questions.prompt: For each shopper in app_logins, return shopper_id and longest_streak: the most consecutive calendar days on which they logged in.
questions.rationale: Find runs of consecutive days. Gaps-and-islands: deduplicate, derive a group key from dates minus row numbers, then aggregate twice.
edgeCases: Several logins on the same day count as one day.
Streaks may cross a month boundary.
hints: Start from SELECT DISTINCT shopper_id, login_date.
julianday(login_date) − ROW_NUMBER() is constant within a run of consecutive days.
Count rows per (shopper, run key), then take the MAX per shopper.
questions.solution: WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT shopper_id, login_date FROM app_logins), g AS (SELECT shopper_id, julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp FROM d), runs AS (SELECT shopper_id, COUNT(*) AS len FROM g GROUP BY shopper_id, grp) SELECT shopper_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak FROM runs GROUP BY shopper_id

questions.title: Salary at the time of each review
questions.difficultyWhy: As-of lookup over half-open, open-ended intervals with overlapping bad data and missing history.
questions.prompt: For every performance review, return review_id, employee_id, review_date and salary_at_review: the salary from salary_history whose period contains the review date.
questions.rationale: Join facts to the history version valid at the event date. As-of lookup over half-open, open-ended intervals with overlapping bad data and missing history.
edgeCases: A period covers a date when valid_from ≤ date and (valid_to is NULL or date < valid_to).
If more than one period covers the date (bad data), use the one with the latest valid_from.
If no period covers it, salary_at_review is NULL — keep the review.
rejectedApproaches: duplicates on overlaps and drops uncovered reviews
hints: Today's salary in employees is not the salary at review time.
A correlated subquery with ORDER BY valid_from DESC LIMIT 1 picks one version.
Half-open: a review on the day a raise starts gets the new salary.
questions.solution: SELECT r.id AS review_id, r.employee_id, r.review_date, (SELECT h.salary FROM salary_history h WHERE h.employee_id = r.employee_id AND h.valid_from <= r.review_date AND (h.valid_to IS NULL OR r.review_date < h.valid_to) ORDER BY h.valid_from DESC LIMIT 1) AS salary_at_review FROM performance_reviews r

questions.title: Detect overlapping history periods
questions.difficultyWhy: Interval-overlap logic on a self-join with half-open bounds, open ends and no duplicate pairs.
questions.prompt: Within one employee's salary_history, periods must not overlap. Return employee_id, first_from and second_from for every pair of overlapping periods, where first_from is the earlier valid_from.
questions.rationale: Validate that history intervals don't overlap. Interval-overlap logic on a self-join with half-open bounds, open ends and no duplicate pairs.
edgeCases: A period runs from valid_from up to but not including valid_to; NULL valid_to means it is still open.
Periods that touch (one ends the day the next starts) do not overlap.
Report each overlapping pair once.
rejectedApproaches: pairs reported twice / in both orders
hints: Self-join salary_history on employee_id.
Ordering the pair with a.valid_from < b.valid_from reports it once.
They overlap when b starts before a ends: a.valid_to IS NULL OR b.valid_from < a.valid_to.
questions.solution: SELECT a.employee_id, a.valid_from AS first_from, b.valid_from AS second_from FROM salary_history a JOIN salary_history b ON b.employee_id = a.employee_id AND a.valid_from < b.valid_from WHERE a.valid_to IS NULL OR b.valid_from < a.valid_to

questions.title: Management chain for every employee
questions.difficultyWhy: A recursive walk of a hierarchy with several roots, carrying depth and a path string.
questions.prompt: Starting from every employee with no manager, return id, name, level (top = 1) and chain: the names from the top of the hierarchy down to the employee, joined by ' > '.
questions.rationale: Traverse a tree with a recursive CTE. A recursive walk of a hierarchy with several roots, carrying depth and a path string.
edgeCases: There can be more than one person with no manager — each starts their own tree.
A top-level chain is just that person's name.
hints: Anchor: SELECT id, name, 1, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
Recursive step: join employees e ON e.manager_id = tree.id, adding 1 to level and ' > ' || e.name to chain.
questions.solution: WITH RECURSIVE tree(id, name, level, chain) AS (SELECT id, name, 1, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, tree.level + 1, tree.chain || ' > ' || e.name FROM employees e JOIN tree ON e.manager_id = tree.id) SELECT id, name, level, chain FROM tree

questions.title: Median order value by region
questions.difficultyWhy: No MEDIAN in SQLite: needs order totals, per-group positions and correct even/odd handling.
questions.prompt: An order's value is the sum of quantity × unit_price over its lines. For non-cancelled orders, return region and median_order_value per shopper region.
questions.rationale: Compute a median with window functions. No MEDIAN in SQLite: needs order totals, per-group positions and correct even/odd handling.
edgeCases: With an odd number of orders, the median is the middle value; with an even number, the average of the two middle values.
Exclude shoppers with no region.
Round to 2 decimals.
rejectedApproaches: even counts use one middle value
hints: Compute order values in a CTE.
ROW_NUMBER() and COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY region) give each value's position and the group size.
Keep positions (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 — integer division makes them equal when n is odd.
questions.solution: WITH v AS (SELECT s.region, o.id, SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS value FROM sales_orders o JOIN shoppers s ON s.id = o.shopper_id JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' AND s.region IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.id), r AS (SELECT region, value, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY value, id) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS n FROM v) SELECT region, ROUND(AVG(value), 2) AS median_order_value FROM r WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2) GROUP BY region

questions.title: Build a region history from snapshots
questions.difficultyWhy: Gaps-and-islands with NULL as a real value, non-adjacent repeats, and LEAD for end dates (an SCD Type 2 build).
questions.prompt: shopper_snapshots records each shopper's region at month end. Return shopper_id, region, valid_from and valid_to — one row per unbroken run of the same region.
questions.rationale: Compress snapshots into change history. Gaps-and-islands with NULL as a real value, non-adjacent repeats, and LEAD for end dates (an SCD Type 2 build).
edgeCases: valid_from is the run's first snapshot_date; valid_to is the first snapshot_date of the shopper's next run, or NULL for the latest run.
A missing region (NULL) is its own value: consecutive NULL snapshots form one run.
If a shopper returns to an earlier region later, that's a new run.
rejectedApproaches: <> ignores changes to and from NULL
hints: Mark a row as a new run when its region differs from the previous snapshot's. Use IS NOT (not <>) so NULLs compare as values.
A running SUM of those marks numbers the runs.
Group by run, then LEAD(valid_from) gives valid_to.
questions.solution: WITH marked AS (SELECT shopper_id, snapshot_date, region, CASE WHEN LAG(snapshot_date) OVER w IS NULL OR LAG(region) OVER w IS NOT region THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS starts FROM shopper_snapshots WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY snapshot_date)), numbered AS (SELECT *, SUM(starts) OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY snapshot_date) AS run FROM marked), runs AS (SELECT shopper_id, run, MIN(region) AS region, MIN(snapshot_date) AS valid_from FROM numbered GROUP BY shopper_id, run) SELECT shopper_id, region, valid_from, LEAD(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY valid_from) AS valid_to FROM runs

questions.title: Reconcile orders, payments and refunds
questions.difficultyWhy: Three child tables at different grains, classification rules, and NULL/rounding handling.
questions.prompt: For every non-cancelled order, compute order_total (lines), paid (payments) and refunded (refunds), and classify payment_check: 'unpaid' when nothing was paid, 'underpaid' when paid < order_total, 'overpaid' when paid > order_total, otherwise 'ok'. Return id, order_total, paid, refunded and payment_check for orders that are not 'ok'.
questions.rationale: Reconcile several sources without double counting and classify mismatches. Three child tables at different grains, classification rules, and NULL/rounding handling.
edgeCases: Missing payments or refunds count as 0.
Round order_total, paid and refunded to 2 decimals and classify using the rounded values.
Refunds don't change payment_check (a refund is a separate event).
hints: Aggregate each child table to one row per order before joining.
LEFT JOIN payments and refunds so unpaid orders survive.
Classify in a CASE, then filter on it in an outer query.
questions.solution: WITH t AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS order_total FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id), p AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS paid FROM order_payments GROUP BY order_id), r AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS refunded FROM order_refunds GROUP BY order_id), checked AS (SELECT o.id, t.order_total, COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS paid, COALESCE(r.refunded, 0) AS refunded, CASE WHEN COALESCE(p.paid, 0) = 0 THEN 'unpaid' WHEN COALESCE(p.paid, 0) < t.order_total THEN 'underpaid' WHEN COALESCE(p.paid, 0) > t.order_total THEN 'overpaid' ELSE 'ok' END AS payment_check FROM sales_orders o JOIN t ON t.order_id = o.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.order_id = o.id LEFT JOIN r ON r.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled') SELECT id, order_total, paid, refunded, payment_check FROM checked WHERE payment_check <> 'ok'

questions.title: Design a purchase lookup index
questions.difficultyWhy: Choose equality-prefix and range-key order, preserve a half-open boundary, and satisfy a catalog plus plan contract.
questions.prompt: Retail needs the purchases for shopper 42 on January 4, 2025. Create a full index with exactly (shopper_id, event_kind, event_at), in that order, then return id, event_at and amount for those purchases. The submitted SELECT must use an indexed search through that index.
questions.rationale: Combine two equality predicates and a timestamp range in a composite index. Choose equality-prefix and range-key order, preserve a half-open boundary, and satisfy a catalog plus plan contract.
edgeCases: Use event_kind = purchase and the half-open timestamp interval [2025-01-04 00:00:00, 2025-01-05 00:00:00).
Order by event_at, then id, ascending. Choose any index name; do not change source rows.
This controlled archive contains 12,005 rows. Indexed access is the learning objective, not a claim about elapsed execution time.
rejectedApproaches: Returns the right rows without creating the required index.
Puts the range key before the second equality key.
Creates the index but scans the table instead of using it.
Includes the next day at midnight.

Compare the stored ISO timestamp directly with the lower and upper bounds.
questions.solution:
CREATE INDEX purchase_lookup ON market_query_log(shopper_id,event_kind,event_at);SELECT id,event_at,amount FROM market_query_log
WHERE shopper_id=42 AND event_kind='purchase'
AND event_at>='2025-01-04 00:00:00' AND event_at<'2025-01-05 00:00:00'
ORDER BY event_at,id

questions.title: Cover the event export
questions.difficultyWhy: Separate filter keys from payload columns and demonstrate covering access while preserving a time boundary.
questions.prompt: Export event_at and amount for shopper 7 on January 4, 2025. Create a full index with exactly (shopper_id, event_at, amount) and make the final query use a covering indexed search.
questions.rationale: Build an index that supplies the selected payload without a table lookup. Separate filter keys from payload columns and demonstrate covering access while preserving a time boundary.
edgeCases: Use the half-open interval [2025-01-04 00:00:00, 2025-01-05 00:00:00). Order by event_at then amount, ascending.
Choose any index name. Keep the source data unchanged. This task checks covering access, not execution time.

Does not use the covering index.

Keep the equality key first, the range key second, and the exported amount last.
questions.solution:
CREATE INDEX covered ON market_query_log(shopper_id,event_at,amount);SELECT event_at,amount FROM market_query_log WHERE shopper_id=7
AND event_at>='2025-01-04 00:00:00' AND event_at<'2025-01-05 00:00:00' ORDER BY event_at,amount

questions.title: Make the event-day filter SARGable
questions.difficultyWhy: Rewrite a function-wrapped timestamp predicate as a half-open range and verify the resulting access.
questions.prompt: The starting approach is SELECT id,event_at,amount FROM market_query_log WHERE date(event_at)='2025-01-04' ORDER BY event_at,id. Rewrite the filter, create a full index on exactly (event_at), and return the same rows using an indexed search.
questions.rationale: Preserve day-filter semantics while enabling a timestamp index search. Rewrite a function-wrapped timestamp predicate as a half-open range and verify the resulting access.
edgeCases: Timestamps are normalized UTC ISO strings. Include midnight on January 4, exclude midnight on January 5.
Order by event_at then id ascending. Do not change source rows or use an expression index.
rejectedApproaches: Leaves a function on the indexed column: correct output, wrong access.
hints: Wrapping the indexed column in date() prevents a normal timestamp range search.
Compare event_at itself to the start of the day and the start of the next day.
questions.solution:
CREATE INDEX event_time ON market_query_log(event_at);SELECT id,event_at,amount FROM market_query_log
WHERE event_at>='2025-01-04 00:00:00' AND event_at<'2025-01-05 00:00:00' ORDER BY event_at,id

questions.title: Top events without a temporary sort
questions.difficultyWhy: Align equality filtering, two descending sort keys and a deterministic top-N boundary with index traversal.
questions.prompt: Return the eight highest-amount events for shopper 5, breaking ties by larger id first. Build a full index with exactly (shopper_id, amount, id). Require an indexed search and no temporary sorting B-tree in the final plan.
questions.rationale: Use reverse index traversal to satisfy a tie-broken top-N request without a temporary B-tree. Align equality filtering, two descending sort keys and a deterministic top-N boundary with index traversal.
edgeCases: Order by amount DESC, id DESC, limit 8. Keep source rows unchanged.
This exercise expressly requires avoiding temporary sorting; no general speed claim is made.

hints: The shopper equality selects one contiguous prefix.
SQLite can read an ascending index backwards when both requested sort directions are reversed together.
questions.solution: CREATE INDEX ranked ON market_query_log(shopper_id,amount,id);SELECT id,amount FROM market_query_log WHERE shopper_id=5 ORDER BY amount DESC,id DESC LIMIT 8

questions.title: A truly ordered workspace activation
questions.difficultyWhy: Combines three event roles, relative-time bounds and bag-to-set output while distinguishing ingestion from behavior.
questions.prompt: Return account_id for each workspace with signup followed by project_created followed by invite_sent, all within seven days of that signup. Equal event times are allowed. Use physical occurred_at timestamps, and return each qualifying workspace once.
questions.rationale: Find an ordered activation path while ignoring duplicate deliveries and late ingestion. Combines three event roles, relative-time bounds and bag-to-set output while distinguishing ingestion from behavior.
edgeCases: Match all three events within the same workspace.
The seven-day endpoint is inclusive.
A workspace qualifies if any valid path exists; repeated event deliveries must not duplicate its output.
rejectedApproaches: Checks stage membership without sequence or deadline.
Accepts an invitation after the seven-day activation deadline.
hints: Join or correlate the event stream in three roles within the same account.
Require signup <= project <= invite, then compare the invite time with signup plus seven days. Return unique workspace keys.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT s.account_id FROM events s JOIN events p ON p.account_id=s.account_id AND p.event_type='project_created' AND p.occurred_at>=s.occurred_at JOIN events i ON i.account_id=s.account_id AND i.event_type='invite_sent' AND i.occurred_at>=p.occurred_at WHERE s.event_type='signup' AND julianday(i.occurred_at)<=julianday(s.occurred_at)+7

questions.title: Identify abandoned checkout attempts
questions.difficultyWhy: Use a same-cart anti-join with a temporal deadline and distinguish attempts from shoppers.
questions.prompt: At the fixed observation cutoff 2025-05-03 00:00:00, list each canonical checkout that had no later purchase of the same cart within 30 minutes. Return checkout_id, shopper_id, cart_id and its deadline.
questions.rationale: Find checkout attempts without a timely later purchase of the same cart. Use a same-cart anti-join with a temporal deadline and distinguish attempts from shoppers.
edgeCases: Deduplicate globally by event_key, keeping the smallest id; a retry may have a conflicting payload.
Use (occurred_at, id) as the total event order; equal timestamps follow id order. All times are UTC.

All provided checkout deadlines are before the observation cutoff. A purchase at the deadline counts as timely. Different checkout keys are separate attempts even if timestamps match. Order by checkout_id.
rejectedApproaches: Lets a purchase of a different cart rescue checkout.
Treats a much later recovery as a timely conversion.
hints: Start from checkout rows, then rule out a qualifying purchase with NOT EXISTS.
A purchase for a different cart must not rescue this attempt.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked_events AS (
 SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY id) AS retry_rank
 FROM market_web_events
), events AS (SELECT * FROM ranked_events WHERE retry_rank=1)
SELECT c.id AS checkout_id,c.shopper_id,c.cart_id,datetime(c.occurred_at,'+30 minutes') AS deadline
FROM events c WHERE c.event_type='checkout' AND NOT EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM events p WHERE p.shopper_id=c.shopper_id AND p.cart_id=c.cart_id
 AND p.event_type='purchase' AND (p.occurred_at>c.occurred_at OR (p.occurred_at=c.occurred_at AND p.id>c.id))
 AND unixepoch(p.occurred_at)-unixepoch(c.occurred_at)<=1800)
ORDER BY checkout_id

questions.title: Audit conflicting event retries
questions.difficultyWhy: Select a canonical row while retaining multiplicity and detecting retries with conflicting payload.
questions.prompt: Report only retried event keys. Return event_key, the smallest id as canonical_id, the event_type from that canonical row as canonical_type, and the number of additional ingestion rows as retry_count.
questions.rationale: Separate logical event identity from ingestion row identity. Select a canonical row while retaining multiplicity and detecting retries with conflicting payload.
edgeCases: Deduplicate globally by event_key, keeping the smallest id; a retry may have a conflicting payload.
Use (occurred_at, id) as the total event order; equal timestamps follow id order. All times are UTC.
Count all retry rows even when their payload differs. Order by event_key.
rejectedApproaches: Takes the smallest event type rather than the canonical row payload.
Counts the original event as a retry.
hints: Rank ingestion rows within event_key by id.
Do not use MIN(event_type): the canonical type belongs to the minimum-id row.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked_events AS (
 SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY id) AS retry_rank
 FROM market_web_events
), events AS (SELECT * FROM ranked_events WHERE retry_rank=1)
SELECT e.event_key,e.id AS canonical_id,e.event_type AS canonical_type,COUNT(r.id)-1 AS retry_count
FROM events e JOIN market_web_events r ON r.event_key=e.event_key
GROUP BY e.event_key,e.id,e.event_type HAVING COUNT(r.id)>1 ORDER BY e.event_key

questions.title: Sessionize retries and exact boundaries
questions.difficultyWhy: Deduplicate before LAG, flag strict inactivity boundaries and use a row-based running sum with deterministic ties.
questions.prompt: Assign each canonical website event a session_no for its shopper. Return shopper_id, event_id and session_no, in shopper and event order.
questions.rationale: Build stable session identifiers from canonical events and inactivity gaps. Deduplicate before LAG, flag strict inactivity boundaries and use a row-based running sum with deterministic ties.
edgeCases: Deduplicate globally by event_key, keeping the smallest id; a retry may have a conflicting payload.
Use (occurred_at, id) as the total event order; equal timestamps follow id order. All times are UTC.

A shopper starts a session at the first canonical event or after a gap strictly greater than 30 minutes from their previous canonical event. Exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session; midnight alone does not split it.
Session numbers start at 1 per shopper and include every event type, including heartbeat and purchase-only sessions.
Order by shopper_id, occurred_at, id; occurred_at is only a sort key, not an output column.
rejectedApproaches: Starts a new session at exactly 30 minutes.
hints: Deduplicate before computing the previous event timestamp.
Flag the first event and gaps greater than 1800 seconds; cumulatively sum the flag with a ROWS frame.

questions.title: Attribute session conversion to first touch
questions.difficultyWhy: Combine sessionization, first-touch attribution and an ordered same-cart funnel without counting event rows as sessions.
questions.prompt: For each first-touch channel, count sessions and converted_sessions, then return conversion_pct rounded to two decimals. A converted session contains an ordered view → checkout → purchase of the same cart within that session.
questions.rationale: Measure session-level conversion using a deterministic acquisition channel. Combine sessionization, first-touch attribution and an ordered same-cart funnel without counting event rows as sessions.
edgeCases: Deduplicate globally by event_key, keeping the smallest id; a retry may have a conflicting payload.
Use (occurred_at, id) as the total event order; equal timestamps follow id order. All times are UTC.

A shopper starts a session at the first canonical event or after a gap strictly greater than 30 minutes from their previous canonical event. Exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session; midnight alone does not split it.
Session numbers start at 1 per shopper and include every event type, including heartbeat and purchase-only sessions.

Attribute the whole session to the channel of its first event. Conversion is binary per session, regardless of how many carts convert. There is no additional view-to-purchase time limit. Include zero-conversion channels. Order by channel.
rejectedApproaches: Counts successful paths instead of binary converted sessions.
Truncates the rate with integer division.
hints: Make one session_list row per session and one converted row per successful session before joining.
Take the channel from the first event, not the purchase event.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked_events AS (
 SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY id) AS retry_rank
 FROM market_web_events
), events AS (SELECT * FROM ranked_events WHERE retry_rank=1), previous_events AS (
 SELECT *,LAG(occurred_at) OVER(PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY occurred_at,id) AS previous_at FROM events
), marked AS (
 SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(occurred_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS starts_session FROM previous_events
), session_events AS (
 SELECT *,SUM(starts_session) OVER(PARTITION BY shopper_id ORDER BY occurred_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_no FROM marked
), positioned AS (
 SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY shopper_id,session_no ORDER BY occurred_at,id) AS position FROM session_events
), session_list AS (
 SELECT shopper_id,session_no,occurred_at AS started_at,channel FROM positioned WHERE position=1
), funnel_pairs AS (
 SELECT c.shopper_id,c.session_no,c.cart_id,c.id AS checkout_id,c.occurred_at AS checkout_at,
        p.id AS purchase_id,p.occurred_at AS purchase_at
 FROM session_events c JOIN session_events p ON p.shopper_id=c.shopper_id AND p.session_no=c.session_no
 AND p.cart_id=c.cart_id AND p.event_type='purchase' AND (p.occurred_at>c.occurred_at OR (p.occurred_at=c.occurred_at AND p.id>c.id))
 WHERE c.event_type='checkout' AND EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM session_events v WHERE v.shopper_id=c.shopper_id AND v.session_no=c.session_no
 AND v.cart_id=c.cart_id AND v.event_type='view' AND (c.occurred_at>v.occurred_at OR (c.occurred_at=v.occurred_at AND c.id>v.id)))
), converted AS (SELECT DISTINCT shopper_id,session_no FROM funnel_pairs)
SELECT s.channel,COUNT(*) AS sessions,COUNT(c.session_no) AS converted_sessions,
ROUND(100.0*COUNT(c.session_no)/COUNT(*),2) AS conversion_pct
FROM session_list s LEFT JOIN converted c ON c.shopper_id=s.shopper_id AND c.session_no=s.session_no
GROUP BY s.channel ORDER BY s.channel

questions.title: Build a replay-safe ledger load
questions.difficultyWhy: Resolve conflicting source versions, preserve newer target records and prove repeated execution is safe.
questions.prompt: Merge market_load_feed into market_ledger. For each external_id choose the highest source version, breaking ties by greatest feed id. Insert missing keys and replace a target only when the source version is at least its version. Return the entire final ledger.
questions.rationale: Implement an idempotent upsert that handles duplicate source versions and late stale records. Resolve conflicting source versions, preserve newer target records and prove repeated execution is safe.
edgeCases: Do not delete target-only or newer target rows. Z starts at version 9, amount 90 and must survive its stale feed record.
Order by external_id. Your complete script is tested twice on the same database to check that it is safe to rerun. This is checked with both the sample data and different data.
The feed is immutable; do not clear it or use a one-shot marker to bypass processing.
rejectedApproaches: Overwrites a newer target with a stale source version.
Works once but fails when the whole script is replayed.
Chooses the wrong source record at a tied version.
hints: Rank feed rows before UPSERT so conflicting versions have one deterministic winner.
Add a WHERE condition to DO UPDATE to protect newer target versions.

questions.title: Enforce the reservation boundary
questions.difficultyWhy: Filter invalid references and storage types before deduplicating, then enforce equivalent rules for future writes.
questions.prompt: Create safe_reservations with shopper_id, item_id and quantity. Load the latest valid feed row for each shopper/item pair, then return the loaded rows. Valid input has existing shopper and item keys and an integer-stored quantity from 1 through 5.
questions.rationale: Separate staging cleanup from durable relational and domain constraints. Filter invalid references and storage types before deduplicating, then enforce equivalent rules for future writes.
edgeCases: Filter invalid feed rows before choosing greatest feed id per pair. A later invalid row must not suppress an earlier valid one.
The target must reject NULL keys, orphan keys, duplicate pairs, NULL quantity, fractional quantity and quantities outside 1–5; valid new rows must remain insertable.
Use a composite primary key, NOT NULL, foreign keys and a quantity CHECK including typeof(quantity). Order by shopper_id,item_id.
rejectedApproaches: Produces correct initial rows but accepts invalid future quantities.
Omits foreign keys: future orphan reservations succeed.
Loads the oldest valid row instead of the latest.
hints: Rank only rows that already passed type, range and parent-existence checks.
SQLite type affinity alone does not guarantee an integer; combine NOT NULL and a domain CHECK.
questions.solution:
CREATE TABLE safe_reservations(
shopper_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shoppers(id),item_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES catalog_items(id),
quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(typeof(quantity)='integer' AND quantity BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
PRIMARY KEY(shopper_id,item_id));INSERT INTO safe_reservations WITH eligible AS (
SELECT f.*,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY shopper_id,item_id ORDER BY f.id DESC) AS rn
FROM market_reservation_feed f WHERE typeof(quantity)='integer' AND quantity BETWEEN 1 AND 5
AND EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM shoppers s WHERE s.id=f.shopper_id)
AND EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM catalog_items c WHERE c.id=f.item_id))
SELECT shopper_id,item_id,quantity FROM eligible WHERE rn=1;
SELECT shopper_id,item_id,quantity FROM safe_reservations ORDER BY shopper_id,item_id

questions.title: Recover a failed stock allocation
questions.difficultyWhy: Recover both stock and audit effects of a rejected batch, preserve history and apply a valid batch atomically.
questions.prompt: The rejected batch cannot fit available stock: its item 2 request exceeds availability. Demonstrate recovery from a provisional reservation of 2 units of item 1 and a rejected audit entry, then apply only the accepted batch. Return item_id, available and reserved from the final stock table.
questions.rationale: Verify recovery by the final state of all affected tables, not transaction keywords. Recover both stock and audit effects of a rejected batch, preserve history and apply a valid batch atomically.
edgeCases: Use a savepoint to undo the provisional stock and audit work, then commit the accepted batch. Your answer is checked by looking at the resulting tables, without requiring particular SQL keywords.
Every stock row starts with available=capacity and reserved=0. Preserve all capacities and the historical audit row (units=5).
End with one accepted audit row whose units equal the accepted feed total, no rejected audit row, and each stock balance adjusted exactly once for its accepted quantity. Order by item_id.
rejectedApproaches: Commits the rejected provisional stock and audit changes.
Returns correct stock but leaves a rejected audit artifact.
hints: A rollback to the savepoint must undo both provisional table changes.
Drive the accepted update and audit total from the feed, including items added by changed data.

questions.title: Measure co-purchased product pairs
questions.difficultyWhy: Self-join a bridge table while eliminating self-pairs, mirrored pairs and quantity weighting.
questions.prompt: Find unordered pairs of distinct products appearing together in delivered orders. Return the smaller item id as item_a, the larger as item_b, and the number of shared orders.
questions.rationale: Count distinct baskets supporting each unordered product combination. Self-join a bridge table while eliminating self-pairs, mirrored pairs and quantity weighting.
edgeCases: Count an order once regardless of item quantities. The order_lines primary key is (order_id,item_id).
Only delivered orders qualify. Order by shared_orders descending, then item_a,item_b ascending.
rejectedApproaches: Counts both mirrored versions of each pair.
hints: Join order_lines to itself on order_id.
Use a.item_id < b.item_id to remove both self-pairs and mirrored combinations.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.item_id AS item_a,b.item_id AS item_b,COUNT(*) AS shared_orders
FROM order_lines a JOIN order_lines b ON b.order_id=a.order_id AND a.item_id<b.item_id
JOIN sales_orders o ON o.id=a.order_id WHERE o.status='delivered'
GROUP BY a.item_id,b.item_id ORDER BY shared_orders DESC,item_a,item_b

questions.title: Find shoppers in every category
questions.difficultyWhy: Express relational division over a dynamic category universe, respecting delivered-order membership.
questions.prompt: Return shoppers who bought at least one item from every distinct category currently in catalog_items, considering only delivered orders.
questions.rationale: Find entities related to every member of a changing required set. Express relational division over a dynamic category universe, respecting delivered-order membership.
edgeCases: Derive the required category set from the catalog; do not hardcode four categories or named categories.
Multiple products and orders in one category count only once. Include every qualifying shopper and order by shopper_id.
This exercise adds two illustrative orders to the standard Retail data; previews include them.
rejectedApproaches: Lets a cancelled order satisfy a required category.
Hardcodes the initial number of categories.
hints: Read double NOT EXISTS as “there is no required category missing from this shopper”.
An alternative is counting distinct purchased categories against the catalog category count.
questions.solution:
SELECT s.id AS shopper_id,s.name FROM shoppers s WHERE NOT EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM catalog_items c WHERE NOT EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM sales_orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id=o.id JOIN catalog_items bought ON bought.id=l.item_id
 WHERE o.shopper_id=s.id AND o.status='delivered' AND bought.category=c.category)) ORDER BY shopper_id

questions.title: Compare category audience overlap
questions.difficultyWhy: Reduce the bridge to shopper/category membership before computing set intersections and unions.
questions.prompt: For each alphabetically ordered pair of categories sharing at least one delivered-order shopper, return shared_buyers, union_buyers and jaccard = shared / union rounded to three decimals.
questions.rationale: Compute Jaccard overlap without inflating membership by line-item or repeat-order counts. Reduce the bridge to shopper/category membership before computing set intersections and unions.
edgeCases: A shopper belongs to a category once, regardless of repeat orders or quantities. Include only pairs with shared buyers.
Use category_a < category_b. Order by category_a,category_b.
rejectedApproaches: Lets repeat purchases multiply memberships and intersections.
Double-counts shared shoppers in the union.
hints: Build DISTINCT shopper_id/category membership first.
The union size is buyers(A) + buyers(B) − shared buyers.
questions.solution:
WITH membership AS (
SELECT DISTINCT o.shopper_id,c.category FROM sales_orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id=o.id
JOIN catalog_items c ON c.id=l.item_id WHERE o.status='delivered'
), totals AS (SELECT category,COUNT(*) AS buyers FROM membership GROUP BY category), intersections AS (
SELECT a.category AS category_a,b.category AS category_b,COUNT(*) AS shared_buyers
FROM membership a JOIN membership b ON b.shopper_id=a.shopper_id AND a.category<b.category GROUP BY a.category,b.category)
SELECT i.category_a,i.category_b,i.shared_buyers,ta.buyers+tb.buyers-i.shared_buyers AS union_buyers,
ROUND(1.0*i.shared_buyers/(ta.buyers+tb.buyers-i.shared_buyers),3) AS jaccard
FROM intersections i JOIN totals ta ON ta.category=i.category_a JOIN totals tb ON tb.category=i.category_b
ORDER BY i.category_a,i.category_b

questions.title: Parse malformed product codes
questions.difficultyWhy: Validate the entire token before extracting typed fields; CAST alone accepts malformed numeric prefixes.
questions.prompt: Normalize raw_code by trimming ASCII spaces and uppercasing it. Keep only codes of the exact form HM-DDDD-AA, where DDDD is four ASCII digits representing 1–9999 and AA is two ASCII letters. Return import_id, integer item_number and uppercase region.
questions.rationale: Normalize and validate a fixed-format identifier before parsing it. Validate the entire token before extracting typed fields; CAST alone accepts malformed numeric prefixes.
edgeCases: Reject NULL, 0000, extra characters, internal spaces and malformed delimiters. Order by import_id.
Region is any pair of ASCII letters, not a lookup against a country list.

Rejects valid lowercase import codes instead of normalizing them.
hints: Check exact length and delimiter positions before casting.
NOT GLOB with a negated character class rejects a non-digit anywhere in a substring.
questions.solution:
WITH normalized AS (SELECT id,UPPER(TRIM(raw_code)) AS code FROM market_raw_import)
SELECT id AS import_id,CAST(SUBSTR(code,4,4) AS INTEGER) AS item_number,SUBSTR(code,9,2) AS region
FROM normalized WHERE LENGTH(code)=10 AND SUBSTR(code,1,3)='HM-' AND SUBSTR(code,8,1)='-'
AND SUBSTR(code,4,4) NOT GLOB '*[^0-9]*' AND CAST(SUBSTR(code,4,4) AS INTEGER)>0
AND SUBSTR(code,9,2) NOT GLOB '*[^A-Z]*' ORDER BY import_id

questions.title: Normalize contact import collisions
questions.difficultyWhy: Apply an explicit normalization and validity contract before grouping, without collapsing meaningful aliases.
questions.prompt: Find duplicate valid emails after lowercasing and trimming outer ASCII spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds. Return normalized_email, source_rows and the smallest source id as first_id.
questions.rationale: Find normalized duplicate contacts while excluding malformed identifiers. Apply an explicit normalization and validity contract before grouping, without collapsing meaningful aliases.
edgeCases: For this exercise only: exactly one @; a nonempty local part; domain has a dot that is neither its first nor last character; no consecutive domain dots; no ASCII space, tab, CR or LF anywhere after trimming.
This is a deliberately limited import rule, not full email-standard validation. Keep plus aliases distinct; do not remove dots or plus suffixes.
Return only groups with more than one valid source row, ordered by normalized_email.
rejectedApproaches: Leaves tabs and line breaks around otherwise matching addresses.
Allows multiple @ symbols and groups malformed addresses.
hints: TRIM can take an explicit character set built with char(9), char(10), char(13) and space.
Count @ characters using the length difference before and after REPLACE.
questions.solution:
WITH normalized AS (
SELECT id,LOWER(TRIM(raw_email,char(9)||char(10)||char(13)||' ')) AS email FROM market_raw_import
), split AS (SELECT *,SUBSTR(email,INSTR(email,'@')+1) AS domain FROM normalized), valid AS (
SELECT * FROM split WHERE LENGTH(email)-LENGTH(REPLACE(email,'@',''))=1 AND INSTR(email,'@')>1
AND INSTR(domain,'.')>1 AND SUBSTR(domain,-1)<>'.' AND INSTR(domain,'..')=0
AND INSTR(email,' ')=0 AND INSTR(email,char(9))=0 AND INSTR(email,char(10))=0 AND INSTR(email,char(13))=0)
SELECT email AS normalized_email,COUNT(*) AS source_rows,MIN(id) AS first_id FROM valid
GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*)>1 ORDER BY normalized_email

questions.title: Parse money into exact integer cents
questions.difficultyWhy: Validate sign, decimal grammar and digit limits, then compute cents without permissive casts or floating-point rounding.
questions.prompt: For every import row, parse raw_amount into cents or NULL and label status valid or invalid. Trim outer ASCII spaces. Accept an optional leading + or -, one to six ASCII whole-number digits, and optionally a decimal point followed by one or two ASCII digits.
questions.rationale: Turn validated decimal text into exact integer minor units. Validate sign, decimal grammar and digit limits, then compute cents without permissive casts or floating-point rounding.
edgeCases: Leading zeros count toward the six-digit limit. Signed zero is valid. Missing whole digits, a trailing dot, exponents, separators, currency symbols and NULL are invalid.
Use integer cents: 19.99 is 1999 and -0.29 is -29. No floating-point tolerance is intended. Return every row ordered by import_id.
rejectedApproaches: Treats permissive casts as validation and uses floating-point money.
Accepts a whole-number part beyond the stated digit limit.
hints: Remove one optional sign, then split the unsigned body at its first dot.
Validate both digit substrings before casting. Pad the fraction to two places, then combine whole*100 + fraction.
questions.solution:
WITH stripped AS (SELECT id,TRIM(raw_amount) AS raw FROM market_raw_import),
unsigned AS (SELECT *,CASE WHEN SUBSTR(raw,1,1) IN ('+','-') THEN SUBSTR(raw,2) ELSE raw END AS body,
CASE WHEN SUBSTR(raw,1,1)='-' THEN -1 ELSE 1 END AS sign FROM stripped),
parts AS (SELECT *,CASE WHEN INSTR(body,'.')=0 THEN body ELSE SUBSTR(body,1,INSTR(body,'.')-1) END AS whole,
CASE WHEN INSTR(body,'.')=0 THEN '' ELSE SUBSTR(body,INSTR(body,'.')+1) END AS fraction FROM unsigned),
checked AS (SELECT *,CASE WHEN LENGTH(whole) BETWEEN 1 AND 6 AND whole NOT GLOB '*[^0-9]*'
AND (INSTR(body,'.')=0 OR (LENGTH(fraction) BETWEEN 1 AND 2 AND fraction NOT GLOB '*[^0-9]*')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS valid FROM parts)
SELECT id AS import_id,CASE WHEN valid=1 THEN sign*(CAST(whole AS INTEGER)*100+CAST(SUBSTR(fraction||'00',1,2) AS INTEGER)) END AS cents,
CASE WHEN valid=1 THEN 'valid' ELSE 'invalid' END AS status FROM checked ORDER BY import_id
